newsitem.title: UK: UK firms miss out on ethnic minority consumers.
newsitem.headline: UK firms miss out on ethnic minority consumers.

text.p: British companies are missing business opportunites by not marketing their products and services more effectively to ethnic minorities, a study released on Monday said.
Business in the Community, a group encouraging firms to help their communities, said companies were missing out on ethnic minority consumers who had 10 billion stg in spending power each year.
The study showed "...businesses are missing out as people from ethnic minorities feel alienated by corporate Britain's marketing and employment approach".

The study by The Susie Fisher Group, a market research company, and supported by Midland Bank, British Airways, BT and Lloyds/TSB, said ethnic minorities were drawn to mainstream brands and institutions such as McDonald's, Cadbury's, British Airways and BT.
"But these marketing opportunities are undermined by feelings of exclusion caused by advertising messages, product ranges, customer service and employement policies," the study said.
It said advertising in Britain often ignored ethnic minorities and sometimes created images they found offensive.
The study found black consumers, for instance, objected to a television commercial for Unilever's Persil detergent that showed a dalmatian shaking off its black spots.
"...the Persil Dalmatian shaking off its black spots proved 'instantly and volubly offensive' to black consumers," the statement said.
Britain's Independent Television Commission said in August it had received complaints the ad carried a racist message that white was superior to black.
The study said ethnic minorities also felt excluded from the mainstream consumer market because of racial discrimination in employment and the way they were treated in stores.
"Ethnic minorities interpret poor customer service as prejudice and some feel they are constantly watch in shops," it said.

Robert Ayling, chief executive of British Airways, said in the statement, "The UK's ethnic minority communities are an increasingly large and important part of our society, but statistics show that while they represent a major business potential, it is largely untapped."

"It is absolutely vital that the leaders of British businesses are involved in attracting them into the mainstream of British commerce by creating new opportunities in employment, marketing and purchasing," he said.
"We will not compete effectively in the global economy unless we harness all of the talent and resources available to us," Ayling said.
